Fish
fish
n. (a creature of the waters; rendering Hebrew dag, Greek ichthus and opsarion)
From the Saxon fisc, cognate with the Latin piscis. The Greek ichthus became the earliest Christian emblem, its letters taken as an acrostic for Jesus Christ, God's Son, Saviour — a sign scratched where a cross would have been dangerous.

Biblical Definition

Fish enter Scripture under man's dominion in the creation mandate: “let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over the cattle, and over all the earth” (Genesis 1:26). The order given to Adam covers the water before it covers anything else. God then uses a fish as an instrument of both judgment and rescue: “Now the LORD had prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah. And Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights” (Jonah 1:17) — the verb is prepared, and our Lord took those three days as the only sign that would be given his generation. In the Gospels fish are the ordinary food that Christ multiplies: “We have here but five loaves, and two fishes” (Matthew 14:17), a boy's lunch out of which a hillside was fed. And after the resurrection, John counts them: Peter “drew the net to land full of great fishes, an hundred and fifty and three: and for all there were so many, yet was not the net broken” (John 21:11). The number is exact because the man who wrote it counted them on a beach at daybreak, and the unbroken net is noted because on an earlier morning, before the cross, the net had broken (Luke 5:6). The risen Christ's draught holds.

Webster 1828 Definition

Creatures of the waters, under man's dominion from Genesis 1. A prepared fish holds Jonah three days — the sign Christ claimed — and the risen Lord's draught fills a net that does not break.

expand to see more

FISH, n. [Sax. fisc; L. piscis.] An animal that lives in water. Fish is a general name for an animal that swims and breathes by gills.

2. The flesh of fish, used as food.

3. FISH, v.i. To attempt to catch fish; to be employed in taking fish.

4. To seek to obtain by artifice, or indirectly; as, to fish for compliments.

5. In Scripture, the fish of the sea are given to man's dominion, Gen. 1; and fishers of men, Matt. 4.

Key Scripture

Genesis 1:26 — "And God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over the cattle, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth."

Jonah 1:17 — "Now the LORD had prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah. And Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights."

Matthew 14:17 — "And they say unto him, We have here but five loaves, and two fishes."

John 21:11 — "Simon Peter went up, and drew the net to land full of great fishes, an hundred and fifty and three: and for all there were so many, yet was not the net broken."

Modern Corruption

The dominion given in Genesis 1 is read either as a licence to exploit or as an embarrassment to be apologised for, when Scripture makes it a stewardship exercised under God and answerable to him.

expand to see more

Two readings of the creation mandate both go wrong. The first takes dominion as ownership and treats the creatures as raw material with no claim of any kind — a reading Scripture contradicts by requiring the ox to rest on the sabbath, forbidding the muzzling of the treading ox, and commending the righteous man who regardeth the life of his beast. The second reading, embarrassed by dominion, effectively denies the ordering of Genesis 1 and puts man among the creatures rather than over them, which cannot be squared with a text that makes only man the image of God. The biblical position is stewardship: real authority, really delegated, and answerable at a real accounting. A steward may use what he manages and may not waste it.

The principle to recover is the sign of Jonah. Our Lord staked his identity on a fish story that modern scholarship has often treated as folklore, and he did so in the plainest terms: as Jonas was three days and three nights in the whale's belly; so shall the Son of man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth (Matthew 12:40). He also said the men of Nineveh would rise in judgment against his hearers because they repented at Jonah's preaching. Both statements assume the events happened. To read Jonah as a parable is not a neutral literary judgment; it removes the sign Christ pointed to when he was asked for evidence.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew dag is a fish, and dagah the collective. Greek ichthus is a fish, the early Christian acrostic; opsarion is the small fish eaten with bread.

expand to see more

Hebrew dag (H1709) — a fish; the fish of the sea placed under man's dominion.

Hebrew dagah (H1710) — fish collectively; the great fish that swallowed Jonah.

Greek ichthus (G2486) — a fish; taken by the early church as an acrostic confession of Christ.

Greek opsarion (G3795) — a small fish, relish eaten with bread; the lad's two small fishes.

Greek ketos (G2785) — a sea monster, great fish; the whale of Matthew 12:40.

Usage

"Of dominion given at creation: let them have dominion over the fish of the sea (Genesis 1:26)."

"Of the prepared fish and the sign: the LORD had prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah (Jonah 1:17)."

"Of the risen Lord's unbroken net: an hundred and fifty and three… yet was not the net broken (John 21:11)."
